subject: multimedia
note: Written-answer review ledger. One entry per written bank question, recording that its modelAnswer, keywords and bandDescriptors were compared against NESA's official sample answer and criteria in data/answer-key/written/. ⚠️ `reviewMethod` says WHO did the comparing and how far a human checked it — do not read an entry as a per-question human sign-off unless that field says so. `sampleAnswerFingerprint` hashes the OFFICIAL answer as at review time: regenerate the key and any review whose official WORDS moved is void, not stale. `sampleAnswerWordsFingerprint` hashes the same text with word ORDER discarded, so a pure re-layout by the extractor is reported rather than treated as NESA changing. See docs/porting-playbook.md section 6. Rebuild with scripts/build_review_ledger.py; never hand-edit.
reviewMethod: assistant-compared against NESA's committed sample answers and criteria rows; NO human sign-off on any question. The six Section III questions were authored by the same session that reviewed them

11.note: Answer and acceptableAnswers match NESA exactly ('Real Time Streaming Protocol'). Corrected only in that it had NO bandDescriptors, so AI marking fell back to the engine's generic 0/50/100% rubric. NESA prints ONE criteria row ('Correctly identifies RTSP'), the degenerate N=1 case: full is that row verbatim, partial and minimal state its non-attainment in the established house style -- authored text, not NESA's, and flagged here as such. Deliberately keeps acceptableAnswers rather than keywords: scoreOne() short-circuits on acceptableAnswers, which is the right mechanism for a one-fact recall question, and keywords beside it would be inert dead data (the VET 2023 16(a)(i) finding).

12.note: Matches NESA (optical systems track markers on the actor, movements in 3D, computers assemble the data to approximate the character's movements). The bank adds infrared cameras and the skeleton model, which is how optical mocap actually works -- an extension, not a divergence.

13.note: NESA's sample answer is a costing TABLE that extracts as run-together layout ('Item Cost per item Number required Cost Paper (ream) $25.00 30 750.00 ...'), so the bank's worked prose necessarily reads unlike it. Compared numerically instead: paper 30 reams x $25 = $750.00, black toner 7.5 rounded up to 8 x $45 = $360.00, colour toner 23.07 rounded up to 24 x $65 = $1560.00, total $2670.00. Every figure agrees, including both round-ups. NOTE a matcher looseness, not fixable per question: the keywords are numeric, and keywordHit()'s kw.startsWith(word) branch means the bare digit '2' credits the keyword '2670' and '1' credits '1560' -- so those two fire on almost any answer containing digits. Same class as the 'pi'/'pipe' looseness noted on VET 2024 19(b). Left as authored; the fix is an engine change, not a content change.

14.note: Content matched NESA (convert to a smaller format, trim unwanted parts, change bit rate, resolution and frame rate). Corrected because TWO of its own keywords -- 'compress' and 'format' -- appeared nowhere in its model answer, so the engine could never credit them; a student writing NESA's own vocabulary was marked down for it. The model answer's last sentence now reads 'converting to a more efficient codec or file format (such as H.265/HEVC instead of H.264, or WMV) applies stronger compression', taking the words from NESA's own sample ('convert to a smaller sized format such as WMV', 'FLV program will also compress MP4'). Nothing else changed.

15.note: Covers NESA's list point for point (links to services, logo, headline with name/purpose/address/contact, site map and return links, photos or graphics, search function, content blocks, social proof/testimonials, special offers/subscriptions) and adds calls to action. Triage flagged 'call to action' as absent from the model answer; it is not -- the answer says 'Calls to action', which keywordHit() credits on the 4-character shared stem.

13.note: NESA's sample extracts as mangled equation layout ('66 355 200 / (8 x 1024 x 1024) = _= 66 _7.91MB 355 200 / 8388608'), so the bank's step-by-step prose necessarily reads unlike it. Compared numerically: 1920 x 1080 = 2 073 600 pixels; x 32 bits = 66 355 200 bits; / 8 = 8 294 400 bytes; / 1 048 576 = 7.91 MB. Every figure agrees, including NESA's own 8388608 divisor route. Same numeric-keyword looseness as 2020 Q13 -- the single-character keyword '8' fires on any answer containing an 8.

14.note: Matches NESA's structure (compression reduces file size for sharing; lossy = smaller files, quality lost, MP4 the example; lossless = quality preserved, very large files, large storage; high-end cameras shoot raw lossless and normally require post-processing; lossy codecs use algorithms to remove still pixels).

11.note: The most consequential defect found in this review, and it cost marks. This 1-mark question asks the student to identify ONE advantage of PDF, but it carried SEVEN keywords with minKeywords 1, and the offline formula is proportional: a student who correctly identified one advantage matched about 3 of 7, and round(3/7 x 1) = 0, so a CORRECT answer scored 0/1. Measured across the subject, it was the only question that scored zero at its own stated threshold. Converted to acceptableAnswers ('formatting', 'platform', 'consistent', 'prevent', 'password', 'unauthorised'), which returns full marks on any one match -- the right semantics for 'identify ONE', and the mechanism the subject's other four 1-mark questions already use. Separately, 'platform' and 'cross-platform' appeared nowhere in the model answer; its first sentence now ends 'software platforms -- that is, they are cross-platform', taking 'platforms' from NESA's own sample ('formatting to be maintained across different software platforms'). Content was correct throughout and is unchanged.

13.note: NESA's sample here is readable prose rather than mangled table layout, and the bank follows it exactly: 550 MB x 8 = 4400 megabits, 4400 / 80 = 55 seconds. 13.note: NESA's sample is a costing TABLE that extracts as run-together layout ('BUSINESS CARD COSTING Cost per unit Number of units required Total $0.85 800 $680 ...'), so the bank's worked prose necessarily reads unlike it.
